chapter_theme: The third quarter of Agappei Siddhar's songs is the work's most radical stretch. Beside the Supreme stands the void; Saivam is the place where self has ceased, and belongs only to those who know themselves; the four Vedas end at the guru's feet and do not see the Lord; there is no root, no three categories, no caste for one who stands as himself, and at the end no self, no Lord and no sadguru either, no mantra, no tantra, and religion itself destroyed. Puja is a ghost and even the Lord is maya; what remains cannot be spoken, and the stanzas say so by saying 'no, no' and naming solitude and the realm beyond speech.
structure_note: 1692 to 1696 set the void beside the Supreme and define Saivam through the guru's raised foot and self-knowledge; 1697 to 1699 counsel the renunciant's stillness and non-seeking; 1700 to 1704 test what is real (silver and copper, awareness as bond, the breath that does not deliver, the far that is no distance, the unmade); 1705 to 1709 deny the Vedas, the root, the eighty-one words and caste; 1710 to 1716 are the great negation, from the hollowed fruit through 'no self, no Lord, no guru' to the realm beyond speech.

1692.reading: Even if you go to the Supreme, demon, you will return to the earth; the place next to the Supreme, you have seen, is the void.
1692.nuance: பரம் (the Supreme, or the highest heaven) is not the end: one comes back from it, as from the sky in 1681. பாழ், the void beside the Supreme, is here the Siddhars' positive emptiness, the place past all forms, while in 1674 it was barren fruit.

1693.reading: What are the five faces, demon, when the five are laid down like cotton? The raised foot of the dance is the guru's foot, you have seen.
1693.nuance: பஞ்ச முகம் is Sadasiva's five faces; பஞ்சு படுத்தாலே puns on பஞ்சு (cotton) and பஞ்ச (five): when the five (elements, senses, faces) are flattened or made soft as cotton, the five faces are nothing. குஞ்சித பாதம் is the dancer's lifted foot at Chidambaram, which the stanza equates with the guru's foot.

1694.reading: There is no stain, demon, in the place where the foot stood; see all that came in the Ganga and become clear.
1694.nuance: கங்கையில் வந்ததெல்லாம் may refer to what the Ganga carries (everything washed down, which the Lord's foot is beyond), or to the Ganga in Siva's hair, so that the foot's place is beyond even his own attributes. The stanza follows 1693's raised foot.

1695.reading: The place where self has ceased, demon, is Saivam, you have seen; for those who stand with flesh ceased there is no defect.
1695.nuance: தான் அற (self gone) defines Saivam as a state of selflessness; ஊன் அற may mean the body-sense gone, or flesh renounced as food. The parallel of தான் and ஊன் suggests the first: self and body both set aside.

1696.reading: Whose is Saivam, demon? It is for those who know themselves; the place where Saivam comes to be is the sadguru's feet.
1696.nuance: The third definition of Saivam (after 1682 and 1695): self-knowledge, located at the guru's feet. The question ஆருக்கு denies that Saivam belongs to a sect or birth, which 1709 makes explicit.

1697.reading: If birth is to end, demon, make no distinctions; those who have renounced stay still.
1697.nuance: பேதகம் பண்ணாதே forbids making differences, of sect, caste or doctrine; the true renunciant is marked not by garb or austerity but by சும்மா இருப்பார்கள், the stillness of 1679.

1698.reading: Whoever wanders, demon, do not you wander; even if the town wanders, seek nothing.
1698.nuance: அலைதல் (wandering, restlessness) is the demon's native motion; the stanza sets the mind's stillness against the crowd's. ஒன்றையும் நாடாதே, seek nothing, is repeated in 1699 and matches 1665's 'join with nothing'.

1699.reading: A river of honey flows, demon, for those who have seen the holy feet; there is no river of flesh; seek nothing.
1699.nuance: தேனாறு is the nectar-stream of the yogis, here given to those who see the feet rather than to those who work the breath. ஊனாறு (river of flesh) may be the body's fluids or the stream of births in flesh; either way the feet replace it.

1700.reading: Can white become black, demon? Can silver become copper? Is there what is? On your oath, you have seen.
1700.nuance: The questions may deny alchemy's reverse (the real does not change into the base) or deny change in general: what is, is, and does not become its opposite. உள்ளது உண்டோ (is there what is) may ask whether anything at all exists, in the spirit of 1685. உன் ஆணை, 'on your oath', becomes a seal in 1722 and 1725.

1701.reading: Awareness abides within, demon, and there is no support; awareness is bond, and grace is what you have seen.
1701.nuance: ஆதாரம் இல்லை denies either any support for awareness (it rests on nothing) or the six adharas of the yogic body. அறிவு பாசம், awareness is bond, sets even knowing on the side of bondage, with அருள் (grace) as the only thing that is not; the stanza compresses more than it explains.

1702.reading: You have mounted the breath, demon; will you not seek the thing of the sky? Even mounting the breath, I tell you, it will not come.
1702.nuance: வாசியில் ஏறுதல், riding the breath (or the horse, in the cipher), is the Siddhars' breath practice. The stanza grants that the demon has done it and denies that it brings வான்பொருள், the thing of the sky; the breath lore of 1688 is thereby set aside as a means.

1703.reading: It is farther than far, demon, and there is no distance at all; look without looking, if the barren karma is to end.
1703.nuance: The paradox of distance (தூராதி தூரம் and தூரமும் இல்லை) is the standard way of saying the Lord is both beyond and within. பாராமற் பார் (look without looking) is the seeing of 1678, which cannot be done by wanting to see.

1704.reading: It is not something made, demon; I have told you what is; will those who saw it tell? Imagination has ceased.
1704.nuance: உண்டாக்கிக் கொண்டதல்ல declares the real uncreated, the Siddhars' அனாதி. Those who have seen do not speak of it, and கற்பனை (printed கற்வனை), the constructing mind, has stopped; 1714 and 1716 say the same of speech.

1705.reading: The four Vedas do not see him, demon; who then will see the Lord? At the end of the four Vedas is the good guru's foot.
1705.nuance: The Vedas are not denied but ended: their முடிவு is the guru's foot, the Vedanta made personal. The question 'who will see' expects that no one does by scripture, as 1725 says no one has seen at all.

1706.reading: There is no root, demon, and no three categories; if there were a root, there would be release too.
1706.nuance: முப்பொருள் are the three categories of Siddhanta, Pati, pasu and pasam; the stanza denies them together with the மூலம் that 1646 and 1656 had posited. The conditional cuts both ways: release is denied along with its ground, as in 1723.

1707.reading: It is Indra's net, demon, the eighty-one words; the mantra is just the same; do not open your mouth.
1707.nuance: இந்திரசாலம் is the conjuror's illusion. எண்பத்தொரு பதம், the eighty-one words, is the pada-adhva of the Agamic scheme, which the Tirumanthiram counts among the paths; here it and mantra alike are sleight of hand, and the answer is silence.

1708.reading: If you would become the void, demon, do not believe what you have seen; I have told you without your asking, and there is no hearing either.
1708.nuance: பாழாக வேணும், to become the void, is here a goal, confirming 1692's positive sense of பாழ். The stanza denies seeing and then hearing as means, and admits that the teaching itself was unasked (கேளாமற் சொன்னேன்).

1709.reading: There is no caste distinction, demon, for those who stand as themselves; even for one who has recited and understood, there is nothing at all.
1709.nuance: Caste is denied to the one who stands தானாகி, as oneself, not argued away on social grounds as Sivavakkiyar does. The second line removes learning and understanding (ஓதி உணர்ந்தாலும்) from the same person: nothing is gained or held.

1710.reading: The sky all around, demon, and all around in the grove of trees; the fruit the elephant ate is the truth, you have seen.
1710.nuance: வேழம் உண்ட கனி is the proverbial wood-apple hollowed by the வேழம் (the gloss reads it as a disease of the fruit, tradition as the elephant): whole outside, empty within. The stanza may say that the world ringed by sky is such a fruit, or that the truth itself is the hollow, the emptiness inside appearances; both readings suit the chapter.

1711.reading: There is no self, demon, and there is no Lord; there is no self, and there is no sadguru.
1711.nuance: The guru, who in 1696 and 1705 was the end of Saivam and of the Vedas, is denied along with self and Lord. The repetition of தானும் இல்லை in lines 1 and 3 makes the denial of self the ground for the others.

1712.reading: There is no mantra, demon, and no impression; there is no tantra, and religion has been destroyed.
1712.nuance: வாதனை is most likely வாசனை (the latent impression, karmic residue), or else torment; some read it as வாதம், alchemy. சமயம் அழிந்தது destroys the religions of 1663 outright, where 1663 only asked where the demon stands.

1713.reading: Puja is a ghost, demon, and knowledge is crookedness; the Lord is maya, and everything is like this.
1713.nuance: பசாசம் (ghost) for puja is deliberate blasphemy; போதம் (knowledge, awareness) as கோட்டம் (bend, crookedness) and ஈசன் as maya extend the negation to the Lord himself. On the chapter's logic this is not atheism but the clearing of every object, the Lord-as-object included.

1714.reading: It must not be said, demon; even if said, it is a fault; no, no: you have seen solitude.
1714.nuance: தோடம் is தோஷம், a fault; speaking of the real is one. இல்லை இல்லை, 'no, no', is the stanza's only content, and ஏகாந்தம் (solitude, aloneness) names the state left when speech stops.

1715.reading: The god of the tattvas, demon, is Sadasiva; all the other gods are forms of maya.
1715.nuance: A momentary return to doctrine: Sadasiva is the deity at the head of the tattvas in Siddhanta, and lesser gods are maya's forms. After 1713 made even the Lord maya, this ranks the gods rather than denying them, so the two stanzas sit in some tension. The gloss printed here (வாசாமகோசரம்) belongs to 1716.

1716.reading: It is not a word, demon; it is in the realm beyond speech; it is not something that fits, and it did not come with me.
1716.nuance: வாசாமகோசரம் is the Sanskrit phrase for what speech cannot reach, as the gloss says. என்னுடன் வந்ததல்ல, 'it did not come with me', denies that the real is the poet's possession or his teaching; it is not carried by anyone.

links.note: Tirumular defines Saivam as relation with Siva, knowing oneself and reaching Siva; Agappei asks whose Saivam is and answers that it belongs to those who know themselves. Both take Saivam out of sect and into self-knowledge; Agappei adds the guru's feet as its place.

Agasthiyar's stanza instructs: join the standing breath to the space, join the chief fire, join sun and moon together; Agappei says that even one who has mounted the breath will not have the thing of the sky come to him. The conflict holds if 2387 means that the breath practice itself delivers the goal; it eases if the breath there is only preparation.

Arunagirinathar asks for that which the four Vedas say they cannot reach even at their height; Agappei says the four Vedas do not see the Lord and that their end is the guru's foot. Both place the real past the Vedas' reach, and both give it through a teacher (Murugan as guru to Siva, the sadguru).

Sivavakkiyar names the place where one stands without mind, life, Shakti, Sambhu, caste distinction, release, root and root-mantra; Agappei says there is no root and no three categories, and that release would exist only if a root did. Both reach a state in which even the ground of release is denied.

Sivavakkiyar asks what caste is, since all water is one water and all gold ornaments one gold; Agappei says there is no caste distinction for those who stand as themselves. Sivavakkiyar argues from the sameness of matter, Agappei from the state of the knower, and both deny caste.

Tirumular says that for those who by knowledge set Nandi in love there is no impurity, no pride, no caste and no good to seek; Agappei says there is no caste distinction for those who stand as themselves, and that even for the learned there is nothing. Both make casteless-ness a property of the one who has arrived, not a social programme.

Tirumular lists eighty-one words, fifty-one letters and seven crore mantras as the way the adhvas came to be; Agappei calls the eighty-one words and mantra alike Indra's net, conjuror's illusion, and says to shut one's mouth. The conflict depends on Tirumular's verse treating the pada-path as real; as a description of what is to be crossed, the two would agree.

Sivavakkiyar asks the fools crying 'puja, puja' where in the self the puja was received; Agappei says puja is a ghost and knowledge crookedness. Sivavakkiyar's attack is a question about the recipient; Agappei's is flat denial, extended to the Lord as maya.

Sivavakkiyar's place without Shakti, Sambhu, mukti and root keeps the Siva-mantra at its close (சிவாயமே); Agappei goes one step further and denies self, Lord and sadguru in a single stanza, with no mantra left standing. The later Siddhar pushes the elder's negation to its end.

source_issues: 1704 line 4 கற்வனை is a misprint for கற்பனை.
1700 line 3 உண்டோ டி and 1731 line 2 மெய்கண்டோ ம் have a space inserted inside a word.
1715: the GLOSSES entry (வாசாம கோசரம் - வாக்குக்கு எட்டாதது) belongs to 1716, which has the word.
1696 onward: the refrain is printed அகப்பேய்! with an exclamation mark, where 1642 to 1695 print it without; the change is editorial, not textual.
1712 line 2 வாதனை is probably வாசனை (impression); the printed form is ambiguous.
